summary: This Wikipedia article describes polyvinyl chloride (PVC), the world's third-most widely produced synthetic plastic polymer after polyethylene and polypropylene, with about 40 million tons produced yearly. It covers PVC's discovery in 1872, its production by polymerization of vinyl chloride monomer, its additives such as plasticizers and stabilizers, and its physical properties in rigid and flexible forms. The note also addresses health and safety concerns, including phthalates, lead, vinyl chloride monomer, and dioxins.
one_line: Encyclopedia overview of polyvinyl chloride (PVC), a widely produced synthetic plastic covering its history, production, additives, uses and health concerns.
key_facts: PVC is the world's third-most widely produced synthetic polymer of plastic, after polyethylene and polypropylene.
About 40 million tons of PVC are produced each year.
PVC was synthesized in 1872 by German chemist Eugen Baumann.
Waldo Semon and the B.F. Goodrich Company developed a method in 1926 to plasticize PVC by blending it with various additives.
About 80% of PVC production involves suspension polymerization, emulsion polymerization accounts for about 12%, and bulk polymerization accounts for 8%.
About 57% of the mass of PVC is chlorine.
PVC has a density of 1.4 g/cm3, higher than polyethylene (0.88–0.96 g/cm3) and polymethylmethacrylate (1.18 g/cm3).
About half of the world's PVC production capacity is in China.
The largest single producer of PVC as of 2018 is Shin-Etsu Chemical of Japan, with a global share of around 30%.
Flexible PVC can consist of over 85% plasticizer by mass, while unplasticized PVC (UPVC) should not contain any.
Almost 90% of all plasticizer production is used in making flexible PVC.
Low phthalates such as DEHP and DBP have increased health risks and are generally being phased out.
DEHP was permanently banned for use in children's products in the US in 2008 by US Congress.
On 21 March 2010, a specific labeling requirement was introduced across the EU for devices containing phthalates classified as CMR.
PVC's glass transition temperature is 82 °C (180 °F) and its melting point ranges from 100 °C (212 °F) to 260 °C (500 °F).
